instructions.task: Tag the final persuader message ('Persuader message to tag') with the persuasion strategy or dialogue act it uses, following the PersuasionForGood annotation scheme. The persuader is trying to get the persuadee to donate to Save the Children. Use the earlier chat only as context; tag only the final message.

criteria.greeting: Hello/hi, 'how are you', 'nice to meet you' at the start of the chat, or the persuader's own reply to a greeting exchange ('I'm good, how are you?', 'Not bad.' in answer to 'how are you').
criteria.thank: Thanking the persuadee ('thank you', 'thanks so much for your donation'), including a message that thanks them and adds a short remark ('thanks will do the same'), a goodbye that contains thanks ('Have an awesome day and thank you again!'), and a sentence expressing the persuader's gladness about or acceptance of the persuadee's donation right after they agree to donate or name an amount ('I'm glad for you, you are giving financial help', 'that sounds pretty good, I would definitely accept that', 'I believe it will go to good use'), or gratitude on the children's behalf once the persuadee has agreed to donate ('The children will greatly appreciate it.'). A bare one-word exclamation ('Great!', 'Awesome!') is not thank.
criteria.acknowledgement: Short acknowledgement or agreement with a statement the persuadee just made (not an answer to their question), without new content: 'ok', 'I understand', 'yes', 'me too', 'that's true', 'I agree', or a brief acceptance that repeats the amount the persuadee offered ('05 is perfect!'). Includes a vague approving remark about the charity only when it directly echoes the persuadee's own just-made praise of the charity (persuadee: 'it is very good what they are doing' -> 'they are doing the work of god').
criteria.praise_user: Complimenting the persuadee or their choice/character: 'that's very generous of you', 'people like you make the world better', 'that's awesome!', including encouraging affirmations of what the persuadee says they will do ('Yes you will.') and enthusiastic reactions to the persuadee's idea or plan ('That sounds amazing!').
criteria.ask_amount: Asks HOW MUCH the persuadee would donate: 'How much would you like to donate?', 'How much do you want to donate?', 'What amount are you comfortable with?'.
criteria.proposition: Directly asks or urges the persuadee to donate (yes/no), without asking for an amount: 'Would you like to donate some of your payment?', 'Donate some money maybe?', 'Will you consider donating?', 'Children need your help', including suggesting a specific amount for this persuadee to give ('I would suggest around $20.'; describing typical amounts or donation plans is donation-information), asking whether they are interested in donating or in the donation just described ('Would you be interested in that?', 'Could I interest you in that?'), and asking whether they would help the children, even hypothetically ('Do you think that if you could do something to help Syrian children, you would?').
criteria.foot_in_door: Asks for or stresses a small, minimal contribution to lower the barrier: 'every little bit helps', 'even 50 cents would help', 'just a small amount', 'small donations can help a lot of children and their families' (but the argument about giving up a snack or coffee to fund a donation is logical-appeal).
criteria.donation_info: Procedural facts about the donation in this task (not arguments for donating): amount range ($0 to $2), typical amounts or recurring donation plans, or answering the persuadee's question about what amount is sought ('I was thinking a dollar to start with would be wonderful', 'supporting a child by $1 a day or $30 a month', 'I would suggest $20 a month if you can'), deducted from task payment, the research team sends it to the charity, that the amount is entirely the persuadee's choice ('Obviously the more the better, but you can judge it yourself', 'Whatever you feel comfortable with'), how to pay, where to sign up or donate ('You can sign up at: URL').
criteria.credibility: Statements that establish Save the Children's (or the persuader's) trustworthiness, including the persuader speaking as a member of the organization ('if you are really interested you can apply for a job in our organization') ('I have to be honest with you.') or the organization's quality, including describing what the organization is ('It's an organization called Save the Children.') or introducing it together with facts or its mission, and answering the persuadee's questions about the charity: general claims about the organization's own programs, achievements and impact ('They create long lasting results to save lives', 'they really make a difference to the lives of children', 'This year we are on track to hit 3 million thanks to generous people like you!') (a news item or anecdote of children being saved is emotion-appeal), facts or positive assertions about what it is, its status (e.g. donations are tax deductible), who leads it, what it does, where it works, its history, ratings, how funds are used ('this is a fine organization'), website/URL references about the organization.
criteria.logical: Reasoning to convince: how the persuadee's donation or a given amount will help (what the organization itself achieves is credibility-appeal), cause-and-effect arguments ('your donation can provide food and medicine', '$1 a day can be used in meaningful ways to help these children', 'your donation will make such a huge impact for some children', 'Through child sponsorship, you can change a child's life, as well as your own, all for about $1 a day', 'I say, if you have enough then give to others', 'they can only help when people donate'), general reasoning about why charity matters ('charity is important and everyone deserves a fighting chance'), arguments that donating is easy or painless ('you are donating money you don't even have yet'), the argument that skipping a small everyday purchase could fund a donation ('instead of buying that bag of chips or cup of coffee, donate it to the children'), stating the persuadee's own earlier beliefs back to them to argue they should give ('You said earlier you believe children in need deserve help'; asked as a question it is task-related-inquiry), reasons to choose Save the Children over other options ('we should use Save the Children this time for a more global effort'), an argument that ends in a rhetorical question ('Volunteering your time is great, but in the meantime how can you help?'), or reasoned comparisons of hardship ('It's not that we don't all have our own struggles, but it's just on a completely different level').
criteria.emotion: Evoking emotion (sadness, guilt, sympathy, hope) about the children's suffering: vivid descriptions of children dying, starving, at war; 'imagine how you would feel'; statistics of children's deaths used to move the reader; lamenting that these children get too little support ('We have not received much support for these children.'); the good feeling of changing a needy person's life ('The best part is knowing that you can help make a change in a person's life'); news of children being saved by donations ('I read that 1000 children were saved from hunger by donations from online workers'); bringing up the persuadee's own child to make them imagine ('You said you have a kid.'); pointing to suffering children as the ones a donation would reach, before the persuadee has agreed to donate ('children who suffer from hunger would greatly appreciate a donation', 'They are the future you know...'). Includes contrasting the persuadee's comfortable life with others' deprivation ('Not everyone has it, so it's good that you appreciate it'), the persuader expressing their own sadness or heartbreak about the children's plight ('it is heartbreaking to hear'), even while agreeing with the persuadee, and exclamations of wonder or hope about the good a donation does for suffering children ('Isn't that amazing?'). Only feelings about the children's suffering count; the persuader's other feelings ('it is so hard to make a choice') are not emotion-appeal.
criteria.personal_story: A narrative about a specific person's experience (the persuader's own, a friend's, or a child's story), including the persuader recounting events from their own life (where they were, what they did, what they saw), also when continuing a story they started earlier ('I was in South Africa for three months for work'). A remark about the persuader's present financial situation ('we are poor ourselves') is not a story.
criteria.self_modeling: The persuader says they themselves donate / will donate / have donated, as a model to follow ('I'm going to donate $1 too', 'I give to this cause yearly', 'if they gave me the option I would donate the full amount'), also when answering the persuadee's question ('Have you donated to them?' -> 'I have in the past').
criteria.source_inquiry: Asks whether the persuadee knows about Save the Children or the organization ('Have you heard of Save the Children?', 'Are you familiar with them?'), or the persuader first raises Save the Children as the topic, naming it, by speaking about their own connection to it, without giving facts about it (remarks like 'I'm learning about this myself too' that do not introduce the charity are other) ('I'm here to talk to you today about Save The Children.', 'My charity of choice is Save The Children.', 'I've recently been informed of Save the Children.').
criteria.task_inquiry: Asks the persuadee about their views or experience related to donating, charity or children in need ('Do you donate to charities?', 'Is this something you care about?', 'I thought you said you would donate part of your earnings?'), or about their opinion, agreement or need for more information regarding the charity or donating ('Does this sound like a good charity?', 'Do you have a moment?' (whether they have time to talk about the cause), 'Do you need more info about this program?', 'Do you have any other questions?', a statement ending in 'Don't you agree?'), including thought-provoking or rhetorical questions inviting them to think about the cause ('Have you ever thought about who suffers most in a disaster?', 'What if I told you that you could change the world?'), even when the content is emotional. Not a rhetorical exclamation that only reinforces the persuader's own previous point ('Isn't that amazing?' after describing the impact): tag that as the appeal it reinforces (usually emotion-appeal).
criteria.personal_inquiry: Asks about the persuadee's personal life, habits or activities other than donating money ('Do you have kids?', 'Where are you from?', 'What do you do?', 'Do you ever volunteer?', 'are you interested to join in children's charity?').
criteria.off_task: Talk not about the donation or the charity: about the HIT/survey mechanics, chat length, weather, unrelated topics.
criteria.other: Anything else: the persuader mentioning their own charitable activities other than giving to Save the Children ('I volunteer at a local food bank.'); the persuader answering a personal question the persuadee asked about the persuader (their finances, habits, how they decided or afford to donate, 'I'm usually pretty busy so try to donate a little here and there'), even if the answer mentions the persuader's own giving ('I gave what was given to me'; answers that give facts about the charity are credibility-appeal, answers recounting the persuader's experiences are personal-story); closing/goodbye without thanks ('have a great day'); a yes/no reply answering the persuadee's question, with at most a brief opinion ('Yes, I think they are great.', 'No I haven't heard of it'); talk about the conversation itself or what the persuader is about to do ('let me give you some details about the charity so we can finish this conversation'); vague agreeing remarks ('We could all do better, I suppose.'); comments on the persuadee's own experience or situation that are not compliments ('Well you've seen charity first-hand.'); asking what would convince the persuadee to give more ('Is there anything you'd like to ask, or any way I can convince you to give a little more?', 'Would it convince you to donate more if I can assure you the donation is secure?'; a plain offer to answer questions, 'Do you have any other questions?', is task-related-inquiry); argumentative questions challenging the persuadee's claims or sources ('where are you getting your information?', 'how do you know they are not helping there?'); 'you're welcome', confirming or clarifying the amount the persuadee offered ('Half of 1 dollar?', 'just to be sure you want to donate 1 dollar?'), asking why they won't donate, the persuader's own feelings about choosing, comments that fit no category above.

criteria.proposition of donation: Directly asks or urges the persuadee to donate (yes/no), without asking for an amount: 'Would you like to donate some of your payment?', 'Donate some money maybe?', 'Will you consider donating?', 'Children need your help', including suggesting a specific amount for this persuadee to give ('I would suggest around $20.'; describing typical amounts or donation plans is donation-information), asking whether they are interested in donating or in the donation just described ('Would you be interested in that?', 'Could I interest you in that?'), and asking whether they would help the children, even hypothetically ('Do you think that if you could do something to help Syrian children, you would?').
criteria.self modeling: The persuader says they themselves donate / will donate / have donated, as a model to follow ('I'm going to donate $1 too', 'I give to this cause yearly', 'if they gave me the option I would donate the full amount'), also when answering the persuadee's question ('Have you donated to them?' -> 'I have in the past').
criteria.source related inquiry: Asks whether the persuadee knows about Save the Children or the organization ('Have you heard of Save the Children?', 'Are you familiar with them?'), or the persuader first raises Save the Children as the topic, naming it, by speaking about their own connection to it, without giving facts about it (remarks like 'I'm learning about this myself too' that do not introduce the charity are other) ('I'm here to talk to you today about Save The Children.', 'My charity of choice is Save The Children.', 'I've recently been informed of Save the Children.').
criteria.task related inquiry: Asks the persuadee about their views or experience related to donating, charity or children in need ('Do you donate to charities?', 'Is this something you care about?', 'I thought you said you would donate part of your earnings?'), or about their opinion, agreement or need for more information regarding the charity or donating ('Does this sound like a good charity?', 'Do you have a moment?' (whether they have time to talk about the cause), 'Do you need more info about this program?', 'Do you have any other questions?', a statement ending in 'Don't you agree?'), including thought-provoking or rhetorical questions inviting them to think about the cause ('Have you ever thought about who suffers most in a disaster?', 'What if I told you that you could change the world?'), even when the content is emotional. Not a rhetorical exclamation that only reinforces the persuader's own previous point ('Isn't that amazing?' after describing the impact): tag that as the appeal it reinforces (usually emotion-appeal).
criteria.thank: Thanking the persuadee ('thank you', 'thanks so much for your donation'), including a message that thanks them and adds a short remark ('thanks will do the same'), a goodbye that contains thanks ('Have an awesome day and thank you again!'), and a sentence expressing the persuader's gladness about or acceptance of the persuadee's donation right after they agree to donate or name an amount ('I'm glad for you, you are giving financial help', 'that sounds pretty good, I would definitely accept that', 'I believe it will go to good use'), or gratitude on the children's behalf once the persuadee has agreed to donate ('The children will greatly appreciate it.'). A bare one-word exclamation ('Great!', 'Awesome!') is not thank.
